ask: Where do the imported topics disagree, and which view should hold here?
why: A recorded choice stops the same disagreement from coming back.

ask: What goal does combining the imported topics serve that neither serves alone?
why: A goal of its own keeps the combined topic focused.

ask: How do the imported topics meet? Which outputs of one feed which processes or decisions of the other?
why: Bridges between the imports make the combined topic more than its parts.

ask: Which things appear in more than one imported topic, perhaps under different names?
why: Each pair becomes a same_as bridge, so the topics read as one.

ask: What are you assuming is true that, if it turned out wrong, would change the plan?
why: Each premise becomes a record, so when one changes the kit shows what rests on it.

ask: What has changed in {topic} since we last spoke?
why: Changes keep the ontology current; old facts are archived, never deleted.

ask: What else should the ontology know about {topic}?
why: Anything you add here can fill a gap the earlier questions did not reach.

ask: What is the first thing you want to produce for {topic}, and who will read or use it?
why: A first deliverable gives the interview a concrete target.

ask: What is the main goal for {topic}? What should be true once it is reached?
why: The goal decides what matters: questions near a goal rank higher.

ask: What is in scope for {topic}, and what is out of scope?
why: Clear edges keep the ontology from growing into neighbouring topics.

ask: Who are you, and what is your role in {topic}?
why: The first answers come from your view; your role says whose view that is.

ask: {name} rests on {other}, which was archived. Does {name} still hold, or should it change too?
why: A premise changed; what rested on it may need to change with it.

ask: Which value of {field} is right for {name}: {note}?
why: Linked records disagree; the kit never picks a side on its own.

ask: Which is right: {name} or {other}?
why: Two facts contradict each other and cannot both hold.

ask: Is the link from {name} to {other} still right? The other end changed upstream.
why: An import update archived or removed one end of this bridge.

ask: How sure are you about {name}? What would confirm it?
why: A low confidence marks a fact to check.

ask: What is the {field} of {name}?
why: Records like this one usually say it; until they do, the gap stays open.

ask: What do we know about {name}? Open point: {note}
why: A recorded unknown waits for an answer.

ask: How does {name} connect to other things in {topic}?
why: A node without links cannot be reached from the rest of the topic.

ask: What should a newcomer know about {name}? One or two sentences are enough.
why: A name alone says too little to use.

ask: Is {name} right as drafted? Many records in {topic} link to it.
why: Many links depend on this draft.

ask: What questions about {topic} are still open, or where do people disagree?
why: Open questions become nodes, so they stay tracked until someone answers them.

ask: What are the main kinds of things in {topic}? Name a few, with one example of each.
why: The kinds you name become the topic's own vocabulary, so later answers are filed under your words.

ask: Do people use different names for the same thing in {topic}? Which names mean the same?
why: Other names become aliases, so a search finds a thing under every name.

ask: Which words or abbreviations in {topic} would confuse a newcomer, and what does each mean?
why: Shared words make every later answer easier to file.
